result: The authors developed an automated behavioral detection system using YOLOv5 to measure social behaviors from video, achieving high precision (mAP = 0.97 at IoU = 0.5).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly praised this methodological advance, stating 'The use of YOLOv5 for automatic behavioral detection is an exceptional methodological advance.' Reviewer 1 also noted 'The evaluation of social interactions were successfully performed based on an automated target detection algorithm.' No concerns were raised about the detection accuracy.

result: Distractor faces significantly impacted behavioral performance across all subjects, with distractor biases negatively correlated with social engagement indices (SEI). Individuals with higher SEIs (more social monkeys) showed reduced distraction by social information.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these core findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 noted 'the monkeys with higher SEIs (i.e., more social individuals) were less distracted by the faces of other monkeys' as a key result. The editor described the work as 'convincing,' indicating acceptance of these central claims.

result: Distractor biases toward in-group monkey faces were significantly smaller than those toward out-group faces across subjects and experimental days. Less social monkeys showed greater vigilance to out-group monkeys, while the most social monkey was equally vigilant to both groups.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 summarized this finding stating 'These effects were enhanced when the distractors were out-group monkey faces rather than in-group ones.' No reviewer challenged the in-group/out-group distinction or the statistical robustness of these findings.

result: Attention to both in-group and out-group monkeys correlated with social engagement scores across three dimensions (aggression, grooming, proximity), with aggression showing the highest correlation (r ≈ -0.8). Model fitting revealed different optimal weights for these dimensions depending on whether distractors were in-group or out-group.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 expressed confusion about interpreting weight differences across conditions, asking 'Does this mean that the proximity is indeed the type of behavior most affected in the out-group condition compared to the in-group condition?' and noting that 'some in-group effects such as those involving OT can be tested, which possibly provides good insights.' This indicates uncertainty about the interpretation of these weight differences.

result: Oxytocin administration significantly increased distractor bias toward out-group monkey faces but not in-group faces, with no effects on oculomotor behavior in trials without distractors or on the probability of first orienting movements.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 summarized this finding stating 'oxytocin administration increased the impact of the out-group monkey faces in the social interference task.' The editor noted 'The findings that oxytocin altered social attention and its relationship to both social tendencies and dyadic relationships are important.' No concerns were raised about these specific effects.

result: Oxytocin reduced the impacts of multi-dimensional social tendencies on social attention, with larger effects for in-group distractors and the strongest blunting of the relationship between grooming and attentional capture.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'oxytocin administration...reducing the magnitude of general social tendencies measured with SEI' but also raised concerns about variability and consistency, asking 'shouldn't the weights in Fig. 3f and Figs. 4g and 4h (saline) be expected to be similar, if not the same?' This suggests uncertainty about the reliability and interpretation of these oxytocin effects on SEI.

result: Individual engagement index (IEI) showed strong correlation with distractor bias (r=0.69), with aggression being the most strongly associated dimension. Oxytocin doubled the weight for aggression in the IEI model and reduced the slope between IEI and distractor biases.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings about dyadic relationships. Reviewer 1 noted the study examined 'dyadic relationships among four monkeys' and the editor highlighted that 'oxytocin altered social attention and its relationship to both social tendencies and dyadic relationships' as important findings. No specific concerns were raised about the IEI analysis.

result: The study used four adult male rhesus macaques housed together for at least 4 years, with the authors acknowledging that conclusions may be constrained by the small sample size.
evaluation: Both Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 2 raised concerns about sample size. Reviewer 2 stated 'The study's conclusions are based on observations of only four monkeys, which limits the generalizability of the findings. Larger sample sizes could strengthen the validity of the results.' This limitation was acknowledged but raises uncertainty about generalizability.

result: Subjects were familiarized with all distractor images daily for 8 weeks before the study to rule out novelty effects.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted concerns about 'The limited set of stimulus images (in-group and out-group faces)' but did not challenge the familiarization procedure itself. The familiarization protocol was accepted as appropriate for controlling novelty effects.

result: Response times were faster when monkey faces were congruent with the target compared to scrambled images, and slower when incongruent with monkey faces versus scrambled versions.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 praised the 'Well-designed and robust experiments in the laboratory environment that are linked nicely with the general social tendencies observed in spontaneous behaviors.' These basic distractor effects were not questioned by any reviewer.

result: There was no relationship between SEIs and performance in visual motor trials without monkey face distractors, ruling out impacts of social tendencies on general oculomotor functions.
evaluation: This control analysis was not challenged by reviewers. It serves as an important control demonstrating specificity of the social attention effects, and reviewers accepted the overall experimental design as robust.
